query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new predictive approach that decouples the lattice and electronic heat transport will accurately forecast the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr by explicitly modeling anharmonic lattice dynamics via machine‐learning–augmented ab initio calculations. This method is expected to outperform earlier Debye temperature-based or average force constant models by providing a clearer separation of phonon transport from electron contributions.
generation.material_initial_state: Defect-free, bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples in their pure state (with one variant containing ~1 wt.% oxygen, as per high-temperature conductivity experiments).
generation.intervention: Apply the new predictive framework that employs high-fidelity, machine-learning–corrected interatomic force fields to calculate temperature-dependent phonon lifetimes and scattering rates, thus isolating the lattice (phonon) thermal conductivity from the electronic component.
generation.conditions: Temperature range from 300 to 1200 K for the primary predictions (where previous total conductivity measurements are available) while noting increased uncertainties below 200 K where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable. Samples should be prepared under conditions similar to those in the referenced experiments (defect-free, with controlled minor oxygen contamination).
generation.structural_mediator: The intrinsic atomic-scale complexity mediated by anharmonic lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations due to high chemical disorder in the refractory high-entropy alloy.
generation.mechanism: The method accounts for complex mass and force-constant variations by explicitly simulating phonon dynamics beyond the average Debye temperature approximation. By integrating machine learning corrections into ab initio lattice dynamics, the approach decouples phonon transport from electronic conductivity, allowing for independent predictions of lattice thermal behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: The lattice thermal conductivity predicted by this decoupled method is expected to match experimental lattice contributions within an error margin of about 10–20%, constituting an approximate 30% improvement in predictive accuracy over earlier analytical/debye-based models. Independently estimated electronic contributions should align with low-temperature (below 200 K) transport measurements.
generation.baseline: Earlier analytical and DFT-derived estimates that conflate lattice and electronic contributions and rely on Debye temperature assumptions, which exhibit uncertainties exceeding 30–40% in the lattice thermal conductivity prediction.
generation.boundary: The method’s reliability is expected primarily for temperatures between 300 and 1200 K in near-ideal, defect-free samples; predictions below 200 K may be less reliable due to the comparable magnitude of lattice and electronic contributions and potential coupling effects. Samples with significantly higher oxygen or defect concentrations might also fall outside the predictive domain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement (the 30% figure) is provisional and subject to experimental verification. Uncertainties remain regarding the impact of minor oxygen content on the separate conduction channels and potential deviations in phonon scattering behavior under varying preparation conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one nominally pure and another with 1 wt.% oxygen. Using state-of-the-art thermal transport measurements (such as inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering to directly probe phonon lifetimes) combined with independent electronic conductivity measurements (e.g., terahertz spectroscopy), separately quantify lattice versus electronic contributions over the 300–1200 K range. Compare the independently measured lattice thermal conductivity to the predictions of the new approach.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity (via phonon lifetime/scattering measurements)
Electronic thermal conductivity (via low-frequency conductivity and spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the lattice thermal conductivity component measured experimentally deviates by more than ±20% from the predicted values across the 300–1200 K range, or if the decoupling into lattice and electronic contributions is inconsistent with direct experimental determination, the hypothesis is falsified.

Tailoring the physical properties of Ni-based single-phase equiatomic alloys by modifying the chemical complexity

Abstract: Equiatomic alloys (e.g. high entropy alloys) have recently attracted considerable interest due to their exceptional properties, which might be closely related to their extreme disorder induced by the chemical complexity. In order to understand the effects of chemical complexity on their fundamental physical properties, a family of (eight) Ni-based, face-center-cubic (FCC), equiatomic alloys, extending from elemental Ni to quinary high entropy alloys, has been synthesized, and their electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties are systematically investigated in the range of 4–300 K by combining experiments with ab initio Korring-Kohn-Rostoker coherent-potential-approximation (KKR-CPA) calculations. The scattering of electrons is significantly increased due to the chemical (especially magnetic) disorder. It has weak correlation with the number of elements but strongly depends on the type of elements. Snoek-type damping performance in strong and ductile high-entropy alloys

Abstract: We developed high-temperature high-damping high-entropy alloys with superior mechanical properties via Snoek relaxation. Noise and mechanical vibrations not only cause damage to devices, but also present major public health hazards. High-damping alloys that eliminate noise and mechanical vibrations are therefore required. Yet, low operating temperatures and insufficient strength/ductility ratios in currently available high-damping alloys limit their applicability. Using the concept of high-entropy alloy (HEA), we present a class of high-damping materials. The design is based on refractory HEAs, solid-solutions doped with either 2.0 atomic % oxygen or nitrogen, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2. Via Snoek relaxation and ordered interstitial complexes mediated strain hardening, the damping capacity of these HEAs is as high as 0.030, and the damping peak reaches up to 800 K. The model HEAs also exhibit a high tensile yield strength of ~1400 MPa combined with a large ductility of ~20%. Investigation of PbSnTeSe High-Entropy Thermoelectric Alloy: A DFT Approach

Abstract: Thermoelectric materials have attracted extensive attention because they can directly convert waste heat into electric energy. As a brand-new method of alloying, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in the fields of materials science and engineering. Recent researches have found that HEAs could be potentially good thermoelectric (TE) materials. In this study, special quasi-random structures (SQS) of PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloys consisting of 64 atoms have been generated. The thermoelectric transport properties of the highest-entropy PbSnTeSe-optimized structure were investigated by combining calculations from first-principles density-functional theory and on-the-fly machine learning with the semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory and Green–Kubo theory. The results demonstrate that PbSnTeSe HEA has a very low lattice thermal conductivity. The electrical conductivity, thermal electronic conductivity and Seebeck coefficient have been evaluated for both n-type and p-type doping.
